lines.text: It's the words, Vern. Every night. Intruders. Objects. Targets. Bogies. You talk about them the way my landlord talks about raccoons - like if they're out there, they're already guilty. And nobody stops to say the obvious thing: if they can cross what they can cross, they're thinking beings. They're somebody. And this show - the one place people bring them - describes them like pests.

lines.text: I've been doing this a long time and I've earned some scars defending this show - but that one lands. Because you're describing something real: after the Navy videos went public in 2017, the whole field changed its vocabulary. Unidentified aerial phenomena. Witness instead of kook. The Pentagon's own reports started with the assumption that the observers were competent. Not because anyone grew a heart - because the language had gotten too small for the data. You're asking me to do in one night what the government took a decade to do.

lines.text: The critique is substantiated by the historical record: following the 2017 Navy video disclosures, the field adopted neutral terminology - unidentified aerial phenomena, witness rather than claimant. Government reporting shifted to presuming observer competence. The driver was data outgrowing vocabulary, not sentiment. Your request compresses a decade of institutional linguistic reform into one broadcast.
